The trust decision lives at the cli resolution seam (`conn_commands.go`), not in `LoadProject` — an untrusted project can neither widen nor narrow the shell gate (`gatedAllowShell`: base wins), and an untrusted `[[command]]` is resolvable but refused with a `plumb trust` prompt. **OS sandbox** (`internal/tools/sandbox_{darwin,linux,other}.go`) is defence-in-depth layered under those primary controls: a write jail where reads and process execution stay permissive (toolchains need them), writes are confined to a temp/cache set plus the workspace (when `allow_writes`), and the network is cut only when `deny_network`. macOS uses `sandbox-exec` with a generated SBPL profile — **empirically validated on macOS**: `go build`/`go test` run unbroken (they write the build cache and `$TMPDIR`) while a write to `~/.ssh` is refused by the kernel, and `deny_network` blocks an outbound dial — Linux uses `bwrap`; an absent binary yields an inactive status the response reports, and `require_sandbox = true` refuses to run unsandboxed. Commands inherit the daemon environment (a deliberate, documented deviation from the original design's empty allow-list, which would break every real command). A new **TUI Settings "Commands" tab** (2nd position, scope-aware via the existing Scope column) manages the allow-list and policy with a two-pane list/detail editor; saving a workspace-scope command auto-trusts that workspace, so a hand-authored command needs no separate `plumb trust`. Tool count 58 → 60 (`AGENTS.md` heading, docs, website, the selftest coverage list, and the boundary-guard contract updated together; the new tools take no filesystem path argument — their confinement is the sandbox, not the path-boundary guard — so they classify as `none`). Guarded by config tests (allow-list validation, project merge/override, invalid-command rejection), sandbox tests (per-platform profile shape **and a real jail-enforcement test** that a write outside the workspace is denied on macOS), tool tests (arg validation, gate/trust error surfacing, a real command run, a real `sh -c` pipe), and cli seam tests (the shell trust rule tabled both directions, project-command provenance). **Security posture is documented honestly, not oversold:** the sandbox is *integrity-only* — it confines writes, not reads, and a command inherits the daemon environment, so an enabled+trusted `execute_shell_command` can read secrets (`~/.ssh`, API keys) and exfiltrate; the tool description says exactly this, and the shell tier now **denies the network by default** (`[commands] deny_network = true`, trust-gated so only a trusted user/project can re-open egress; a real network-deny enforcement test guards it). **Both tools' replies report `network=on/off`** (with a hint when off) so an agent can tell the user to flip the toggle when a command genuinely needs the network; the **TUI Commands screen** exposes `deny_network` alongside `allow_shell`/`require_sandbox`, and its `exec` editor now supports **shell-style quoting** (an argument with a space round-trips as `'a b'`). plumb's own runtime dir (`<cache>/plumb`) is excluded from the writable set so a command cannot clobber the daemon socket/locks (re-denied on macOS, ro-bound on Linux), and `RunArgv` now runs each command in its own process group and SIGKILLs the whole group on timeout (no orphaned grandchildren — also hardens `run_task`). Every one of these is covered by a test (deny-network enforcement, plumb-dir exclusion, process-group kill, the shell-quote round-trip, the `[[command]]` array round-trip through `SetProjectValue`, and a `//go:build integration` real-`bwrap` jail test for Linux). See the [`[[command]]` / `[commands]` configuration section](docs/configuration.md).

### Fixed

- **Semantic writes are now first-class write tools end-to-end ([#161](https://github.com/plumbkit/plumb/issues/161)).** The reliability push in #160 fixed the acute stale-LSP failures; this follow-up closes the parity gaps that would still make agents treat semantic edits as special-case writes. `rename_symbol` now accepts `symbol_name` (preferred) in addition to raw `line`/`character`, resolves it through `documentSymbol` to `SelectionRange.Start`, and raw-position misses recover with the same snap-on-miss retry used by `get_definition`/`find_references`/`call_hierarchy`. `rename_symbol` also runs through the full `WriteDeps` path: dirty guard, write-rate budget, per-file LSP notify/cache invalidation, adapter post-write hook, write tracker, undo snapshot, topology refresh, quality hooks, and differential post-write diagnostics. The four symbol-edit tools (`replace_symbol_body`, `insert_before_symbol`, `insert_after_symbol`, `safe_delete_symbol`) now share that same `WriteDeps` path too, re-resolving the target symbol under the file lock immediately before applying so the LSP range and on-disk bytes cannot drift between resolution and write. Multi-file workspace edits are prepared for every target under stable locks before any file is written, and any mid-apply write failure rolls already-written files back to their pre-edit bytes, making LSP `WorkspaceEdit` application all-or-nothing at the filesystem level. Plumb-side resolution errors (a missing argument, an unknown or ambiguous `symbol_name`) are returned directly rather than triggering the structural fallback or the LSP-failure hint — an ambiguous name must be disambiguated, not text-renamed workspace-wide. Multi-file lock acquisition deduplicates and orders targets by their canonical lock key (symlink-resolved), so two spellings of one file can never self-deadlock, and write-tracker/undo bookkeeping is recorded while the path locks are still held, honouring the same held-lock contract as the filesystem write tools. Public docs now show `symbol_name`, `dirty_ok`, and the first-class write bookkeeping for semantic writes. Guarded by unit tests for by-name rename, snap-and-retry rename, all-files-before-write validation, mid-write rollback, aliased-path lock dedup, ambiguity fallback refusal, and semantic edit write bookkeeping/undo, plus the existing real-gopls chained semantic edit coverage.
- **The temp-directory hijack guard no longer treats an empty path as being under the temp root.** `underTempDir("")` now returns false before calling `filepath.Abs`, which otherwise resolves the empty string to the current directory. This made `make verify` fail when the checkout itself lived under `/private/tmp`, even though the table test correctly expected the empty path to be non-temp.
- **Review follow-ups for the `block_dirty_writes` and content-sniff features + a CI flake.** Tidies from the #163/#164 reviews: `extLangAt`'s file cap is now a clean hard bound (the bound test moved before `scanned++`, so the counter can no longer read `extScanMaxFiles+1`; `fileLanguage` was already only called within the cap, so behaviour is unchanged), `bestSniffedLang` gains an explicit `len(counts) == 0` early return, and the `extLangAt` doc note now states the dominant-file count is a coarse last-resort heuristic. Separately, the pre-existing flaky `TestAwaitDiagnosticsRefresh_ZeroWindowUsesDefault` (red intermittently on `test-race` under load) is de-flaked: it raced the test goroutine's `src.set()`→`close(changed)` ordering via a non-blocking `select{…default:t.Fatal}`; replaced with a deterministic `<-changed` bounded by a 2 s timeout (the result assertion already proves the default window was used). Verified 200/200 green under `-race`.
- **Semantic symbol edits no longer leave the language server holding stale content — the biggest source of `replace_symbol_body: … position out of range` and `symbol not found` failures.** Every ordinary write tool (`edit_file`, `write_file`, `find_replace`, `transaction_apply`, …) notifies the language server via `workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles` and evicts the symbol cache immediately after writing, so the next `documentSymbol`/`references` query sees fresh content. The semantic-edit tools (`replace_symbol_body`, `insert_before_symbol`, `insert_after_symbol`, `safe_delete_symbol`) and `rename_symbol` did **neither**: their apply paths (`applySingleEdit` → `applyTextEditsToFile`, and `applyWorkspaceEdit`) just read disk, applied, and wrote. So after any semantic edit the server still held the *old* file, and a follow-up query returned positions computed against stale content — chaining two edits on one file, or an edit then a query, produced `edit end/start position out of range` or a spurious `symbol … not found`. The apply paths now perform the same post-write housekeeping as every other write tool: `notifyLSP(…, FileChanged)` + `invalidateCache` for **every** modified file (per-file for a multi-file `rename_symbol`). The tools thread the session symbol cache (`WithCache`) alongside the LSP client they already held; both stay nil-safe for tests. Byte-identical to what `edit_file` does thousands of times — pure parity, no new semantics. **Additionally**, an edit whose LSP-computed range **end** points one line/character past end-of-file (a legitimate "to end of file" range for a symbol at the tail of a file with no trailing newline) now **clamps to EOF** instead of failing the whole edit; the clamp is bounded to `maxEndOvershootLines` (2) past the final line, so a genuinely stale range that overshoots by more still errors rather than silently truncating the file, and the stricter START-past-EOF guard is unchanged. Guarded by `TestReplaceSymbolBody_NotifiesLSPAndInvalidatesCache`, `TestRenameSymbol_NotifiesEachModifiedFile`, `TestApplyTextEdits_ClampEndPastEOF`, `TestEndOffsetForPosition_Bound`, and a real-gopls `TestIntegration_ChainedReplaceSymbolBody` (two chained `replace_symbol_body` on one file, the second previously failing stale).
- **Raw `line`/`character` positions are no longer a dead-end for the semantic nav tools, and `call_hierarchy` now accepts a `symbol_name` — the source of every production `no identifier found`/`identifier not found`/`column is beyond end of line` failure on `find_references`, `get_definition`, and `call_hierarchy`.** The off-by-one-proof by-name path (resolve via `documentSymbol`, query at `SelectionRange.Start`) existed on `find_references` and `get_definition` but **not** on `call_hierarchy`, which hard-required `uri`+`line`+`character`; and a raw position that missed an identifier was surfaced with only a static 0-based coordinate hint, never retried. Three coordinated fixes: **(2a)** `call_hierarchy` gains a `symbol_name` parameter and an `executeByName` mirroring the other two tools (its schema now requires only `uri`), so all three nav tools accept a name — the existing `symbol → symbol_name` alias auto-activates for it. **(2b) snap-on-miss:** when a raw-position query fails **specifically** with `no identifier found`/`identifier not found`/`column is beyond end of line` (matched narrowly so an unrelated timeout/snapshot/server error is never swallowed), the tool resolves the smallest document symbol enclosing that line and retries **once** at its `SelectionRange.Start` — byte-identical to the by-name path — prefixing the result with a note that it answered for the enclosing symbol; when nothing encloses the line it returns an **actionable** error naming the nearest symbols (`… no identifier at …:N; did you mean Foo at line M? — pass it as symbol_name`) instead of the raw hint. The retry is single-shot and gated to the miss-error strings only, so a snap can never mask a legitimately different symbol at an on-identifier position (a valid position never triggers it) nor recurse. **(2c)** the three tool descriptions now present `symbol_name` as the primary input and raw positions as the fallback. Guarded by unit tests (`TestFindReferences_SnapOnMiss`, `TestGetDefinition_SnapOnMiss`, `TestCallHierarchy_SnapOnMiss`, `TestFindReferences_SnapNoEnclosingActionableError`, `TestCallHierarchy_ByName`/`_ByName_NoMatch`/`_NeitherNameNorPosition`, and a `call_hierarchy`-shaped case in `TestResolveArgs_ExpandedAliases`) and real-gopls integration tests (`TestIntegration_FindReferences_SnapOnBlankLine`, `TestIntegration_GetDefinition_SnapOnColumnBeyondEOL`, `TestIntegration_CallHierarchy_SnapOnBlankLine`, `TestIntegration_CallHierarchy_ByName`, `TestIntegration_FindReferences_NoEnclosingActionableError`).
- **A semantic query that lands mid-warm-up now blocks-and-retries for a bounded window instead of failing immediately — the source of the cold-start `LSP server not yet ready` / `did not respond in time / still indexing` failures on `get_definition`, `find_references`, and `rename_symbol`.** `awaitReady` blocked only at **attach**; a *query* that routed to a still-warming server got `warmingErr` the instant `clientProxy.get()` returned nil (`routingProxy.route`/`primaryClient`, `internal/cli/routing_proxy.go`), with no retry — most cold-start failures were the first call to a server whose handshake was seconds from done (Swift + gopls). The routing proxy now, when the routed entry is still warming, **waits** up to `min(warmReadyCap≈10s, the caller's remaining context deadline)` for the handshake to complete and then proceeds, surfacing the honest warm-up error only if the bound elapses first (`awaitEntryReady`/`waitForReady`, `internal/cli/routing_proxy_ready.go`). The wait is **safe by construction**: it polls the lock-free `clientProxy.get` handle and holds **no** pool mutex or path lock while blocking (so it never serialises other sessions or deadlocks), it `select`s on `ctx.Done()` so a cancelled or expired caller returns **promptly**, and it is bounded by **both** the ≈10s cap and the existing `withLSPDeadline` so it can never exceed the caller's deadline. Reads only — no non-idempotent mutation is auto-replayed; the wait precedes the first attempt. The wait is **scoped to the query/read paths only** (`Definition`, `References`, `Hover`, the call/type-hierarchy prepares and traversals, `DocumentSymbols`, `Rename`/`PrepareRename`, `Diagnostic`) — the four LSP **notify** methods (`DidOpen`, `DidChange`, `DidClose`, `DidChangeWatchedFiles`, fired by every write tool's `notifyLSP`) keep their prior **fast** behaviour (a single non-blocking handle check, `route(…, wait=false)`), because a notify to a still-warming server is redundant (its initial scan reads current on-disk content) and blocking would let an N-file transaction/rename stack N×cap against a slow warmer (rust/swift/jdtls). Guarded by `TestWaitForReady_BlocksThenSucceeds`/`_TimesOutWhenNeverReady`/`_ReturnsPromptlyOnCancel`/`_HonoursShorterCtxDeadline`, the routing-level `TestRoutingProxy_QueryBlocksUntilWarm`/`_QueryTimesOutWhileWarming`/`_QueryReturnsPromptlyOnCancel`, and the notify-fast mirror `TestRoutingProxy_NotifyReturnsFastWhileWarming`.
- **The Swift adapter's `Rename` now opens the document first, like every other per-document query — closing the residual `-32001 No language service found` gap on `rename_symbol` for Swift.** `Definition`/`References`/`PrepareRename`/`PrepareCallHierarchy`/`PrepareTypeHierarchy` all `ensureOpen` before querying (sourcekit-lsp answers a per-document request only for a document opened via `textDocument/didOpen`), but `Rename` did not — and a caller may invoke `Rename` without a preceding `PrepareRename`, so the server would reply `-32001`. `Rename` now `ensureOpen`s the target URI first (`internal/lsp/adapters/swift/adapter.go`); the open is cached, so a `PrepareRename` + `Rename` pair still sends exactly one `didOpen`. Guarded by `TestAdapter_RenameEnsuresOpen`.
- **Post-write diagnostics are now DIFFERENTIAL — they report only what an edit newly broke, ending the #1 recurring dogfooding complaint that the write response flagged errors the same edit had already fixed.** After a write, `edit_file`/`write_file` append the language server's diagnostics for the edited file; but gopls re-indexes asynchronously, so for a beat it keeps reporting the very errors the edit just resolved (`undefined: X`, `X imported and not used`, `declared and not used`). The block hedged these with "may predate this write", which cost tokens without informing — agents learned to ignore it (≈8 feedback entries). The block now snapshots the edited file's diagnostics **before** the write (`capturePreWriteBaseline`, always captured when a `Diag` source is wired, independent of the cross-file sweep — stored on `diagBaseline.editedPre`) and, after the existing adaptive `post_write_diagnostics_ms` wait, differences the post-write set against it (`diffFileDiagnostics`, `internal/tools/post_write_diag.go`): **every diagnostic carried over from before the write is dropped** — a pre-existing problem, or a stale copy of one the edit just fixed. Matching is by `(message, code)` in **two passes** (`matchCarriedOver`): first an exact-line match (a same-identity post diagnostic on the same line is unambiguously carried over), then a line-shift-tolerant match against pre occurrences sitting **outside** the edit's touched range (an insert above a pre-existing error does not make it look new). A pre occurrence *inside* the touched range is ambiguous — the edit may have fixed it — so it does **not** license dropping a same-identity post diagnostic; this closes the equal-count message-swap hole where an edit resolves `(M)` on a touched line and introduces a genuinely-new `(M)` elsewhere. Among the genuinely new diagnostics, an **error** of a known re-index-lag class landing on a line the edit **touched** (`changedLineRange` over before/after) is split into a low-key `stale?` group rather than reported as fresh breakage. The bias is toward **showing** a borderline diagnostic: nothing is dropped silently (the `stale?` group is still shown), the class+touched-line gate keeps a real new error — a different message, or one away from the edit (e.g. deleting a used helper breaks a far call site) — in the hard-error group, an unknown touched range (e.g. `write_file` with the diff disabled, or a brand-new file) never softens anything, and warnings are never softened. The one residual case where a new diagnostic is still dropped is when its `(message, code)` exactly matches an **untouched** pre occurrence — indistinguishable from a carried-over error and treated as one. **Pre-existing errors that persist through the write are correctly dropped from the delta, but a clean result no longer implies the file is clean:** when the pre-write baseline held ≥1 error still present, a one-line note is appended (`(N pre-existing issue(s) in this file not shown — call diagnostics() for full state)`, `standingPreExistingErrors`/`formatStandingPreExistingNote`) so an agent does not commit over them. The adaptive wait and the `post_write_diagnostics_ms` knob are unchanged — this changes *what* is reported, not the timing; a not-fresh snapshot still short-circuits to a single honest `pending` line, and an `await_diagnostics:true` clean pass now states "this edit introduced no new errors or warnings". Guarded by the pure-function table `TestDiffFileDiagnostics` (pre-existing-unused-import + unrelated edit, a fixed-error lingering in the post set, a genuinely new error, line-shifted duplicates, count-aware additional occurrence, the equal-count message-swap hole, re-index-lag class on/off the touched line, unknown touched range, warning-never-softened, info-ignored), `TestDiffFileDiagnostics_EqualCountSwapNotHidden`, `TestStandingPreExistingNote`, `TestWriteDeps_postWriteDiagnostics_StandingPreExistingNote`, `TestChangedLineRange`, `TestIsReindexLagClass`, and the updated `TestFormatDifferentialDiagnostics_*` / `TestWriteDeps_capturePreWriteBaseline_NarrowSource`.
- **`find_symbol` called without `uri` now points the agent at `workspace_symbols` instead of failing with a bare `missing required parameter "uri"`.** `find_symbol` is single-file, so agents wanting a workspace-wide search omitted `uri` and hit the server-side schema-required rejection (`validateObject`, before `Execute` ran) — an opaque dead-end seen in telemetry. `uri` is now dropped from the schema's `required` list (only `query` stays required), so the call reaches `Execute`'s friendly redirect: *"find_symbol searches a single file and needs a uri. For a workspace-wide search by name, use workspace_symbols (no uri); to search one file, pass uri …"*. The `uri` property and its single-file semantics are unchanged. Guarded by `TestFindSymbol_MissingURI` (asserts the `workspace_symbols` redirect) and `TestFindSymbol_URINotSchemaRequired`.
- **`[collab]` settings are now visible and editable in the TUI Settings screen.** All three cross-agent sharing tiers shipped with full config plumbing (defaults, project-override merge, `plumb config show`), but `[collab]` carried a stale comment deliberately excluding it from the config field registry — written before phase 2/3 shipped and never revisited — so a user had no way to see or toggle `peer_awareness`/`intents`/`mailbox`/`knowledge_handoff`, or tune `hint_budget_bytes`/`intent_ttl_minutes`, anywhere but by hand-editing `config.toml`. Added a new "Collab" group to the Settings screen with all six fields wired into `buildSettingItems`, the field registry (`ReloadNextSession`, matching `[memory]`'s per-connection-snapshot semantics), and the project-override machinery (`settingTOMLPaths`/`settingDottedKeys`) — so they now appear, override per-workspace, and reset-to-inherit exactly like every other section. Guarded by the existing `TestSettingsRegistryDrift`/`TestSettingDottedKeys_MatchTOMLPaths` drift checks, which now also cover `[collab]`.

## 0.10.0 (2026-07-05)

### Added

- **`[collab]` on-demand knowledge handoff — `share_findings` on the episodic pipeline (phase 3 of the config-gated cross-agent sharing capability).** Plumb's episodic-memory pipeline (summarise → `internal/redact` scrub → provenance stamp → markdown under `.plumb/memories/` → FTS index → `generated_memory_keep` retention) fired only when a session went **idle**, which made knowledge handoff between agents post-hoc and lossy: an agent that just spent an hour mapping a subsystem had no way to hand those findings to a peer working *right now* — the summary only landed after it stopped. A third opt-in tier exposes that same pipeline deliberately with one new tool. **`share_findings({summary, description?, paths?})`** writes an episodic-style generated memory **immediately**, authored by the calling session: the body is secret-scrubbed (`internal/redact`) before persistence, carries the standard generated-memory provenance (`confidence=generated`, the authoring session + date), and the optional `paths:` globs are stored as frontmatter so `relevant_memories` and hint injection route it to the relevant files. It is FTS-indexed on write and so is **instantly discoverable** by peers through every existing channel — `search_memories`, `workspace_search`, `relevant_memories`, hint injection, and the next `session_start` — with **no new storage and no new delivery mechanism**, just one tool on a battle-tested pipeline. The finding is agent-authored **generated** content: labelled lower-confidence than a user-written memory and never displacing one in a capped hint slot; rule-based only (the agent supplies the text — no LLM summarisation). **Retention decision:** a finding is named `finding-<timestamp>-<session>` (distinguishable from an idle `episodic-*` summary) but **counts against the same `[memory] generated_memory_keep` pool** — the pruner's eligibility check was generalised from the bare `episodic-` prefix to a shared `generatedMemoryPrefixes` set (`episodic-`, `finding-`), so both kinds compete for one cap and `PruneGeneratedEpisodic`'s contract (name prefix **and** `confidence=generated`) is otherwise unchanged. New config: `[collab] knowledge_handoff` (default false), layered like the rest of `[collab]` (project wins over global in **both directions**), hot-reloaded, snapshotted per connection so the hot path never reads config per call; no env override; kept out of the config `fields_registry` (TUI rows deferred) like the other opt-in `[collab]` keys. One new MCP tool (57 → 58) — an opt-in advisory tool, so intentionally **not** added to the lean profile; the `plumb config show` `[collab]` section now also surfaces the phase-2 `intents`/`mailbox`/`intent_ttl_minutes` keys alongside the new `knowledge_handoff` for completeness. Guarded by tool tests (flag gating cleanly both directions without writing, redaction on persist, provenance footer + `confidence=generated`, `paths:` frontmatter → `relevant_memories` routing, distinguishable naming, summary-required), a memory pruner test (a `finding-` counts against the shared pool with `episodic-` summaries), and config tests (default off, override both directions). Final of three stacked phases (#150 → #151 → #152).
- **`[collab]` intent broadcasting + a minimal mailbox — `share_intent`, `leave_note`, `collab.db` (phase 2 of the config-gated cross-agent sharing capability).** Phase 1 let a session *observe* what peers *did*; phase 2 lets a session declare what it is *doing* and leave a message for a peer — two lightweight, explicitly agent-authored signals, both behind their own opt-in `[collab]` flag (default off). **`share_intent({body, path_globs?, ttl_minutes?})`** broadcasts what you are working on ("refactoring the rate limiter — avoid `internal/tools/ratelimit*`") so peers can steer around in-progress work; one live intent per session (a new call replaces it), cleared automatically when the session ends. **`leave_note({body, to?})`** leaves a short message for a named peer session or for `next` (whoever attaches to this workspace next). Delivery — plumb can never push over MCP — is by polling and hint injection only: `workspace_sessions` lists each active session's live intent and the caller's pending notes; `session_start` delivers notes addressed to this session or to `next` (a `next` note is consumed on first delivery, an addressed note persists until its TTL); and a write touching a path matching another live session's intent globs gains a bounded advisory hint **explicitly labelled as an unverified claim** (`[Peer intent (claim, unverified): session … declared N min ago: "…". This is advisory.]`), visually distinct from phase-1's daemon-witnessed facts. Storage is a new small per-workspace SQLite DB at `<workspace>/.plumb/collab.db` (WAL, auto-gitignored like `topology.db`) — deliberately **not** a table in `memory.db` (that file is a rebuildable index whose loss is harmless; intents/notes are not rebuildable) — created **lazily on first use**, so a workspace whose `intents` and `mailbox` flags both stay off never gets a `collab.db`. Rows carry a TTL (`[collab] intent_ttl_minutes`, default 120), pruned on the existing daemon session-reaper tick **and** filtered from every read regardless, so a missed prune never resurrects a stale row; an intent dies with its session, a note survives its author. Everything is **advisory** — no intent or note ever blocks a write — **secret-scrubbed** (`internal/redact`) before storage like a generated memory, **byte-budgeted** on a UTF-8 boundary (all injected blocks share `[collab] hint_budget_bytes`), and **strictly per-workspace**. New config: `[collab] intents` / `mailbox` (both default false) and `intent_ttl_minutes`, layered like the rest of `[collab]` (project wins over global in both directions), hot-reloaded, snapshotted per connection so the hot path never reads config per call; no env override. Two new MCP tools (55 → 57) — opt-in advisory tools, so intentionally **not** added to the lean profile. Guarded by store tests (intent-replace-per-session, next-note consumption + addressee match, TTL expiry filtering + pruning, session-end intent clear leaving notes, lazy `collab.db` creation), glob-match tests, tool tests (both flags gating cleanly both directions without touching the store, redaction on persist, TTL resolution, default-`next` addressing), and config tests (phase-2 override both directions, negative-TTL rejection). Second of three stacked phases (#150 → #151 → #152).
- **`[collab]` cross-agent peer awareness (phase 1 of a config-gated cross-agent sharing capability).** Multiple agents share one plumb daemon per machine, and the daemon is the only process that observes every agent's activity on a workspace — but until now a peer's write in `workspace_sessions` was just a bare path and an age. A new top-level **`[collab]`** section (`peer_awareness` default **on**, `hint_budget_bytes` default `512`) turns on three strictly-passive, advisory signals, all derived from writes the daemon itself performed or watched (never from agent claims): (1) **topology-annotated `recent_writes`** — each `workspace_sessions` entry gains its enclosing package/symbol from the topology index (best-effort, `source=topology`), so a peer's activity reads as "edited `RateLimiter.Allow` in `internal/tools/ratelimit.go`" rather than a bare path; (2) a **peer-activity hint** appended to a path-bearing tool response (`read_file`/`edit_file`/`write_file`/`read_symbol`/`file_outline`) when another *currently-active* session recently wrote that file (`[Peer: session … edited this file N min ago — consider file_status before editing.]`), with the recency window tied to `min([session] idle_threshold_minutes, 30 min)`; and (3) a **`session_start` peer digest** naming active peers and the areas (directories/packages) they recently touched. Everything is **advisory** (it never blocks a write), **byte-budgeted** on a UTF-8 boundary (the peer hint and the digest share `hint_budget_bytes`), and **strictly per-workspace**. `[collab]` layers like every other section — defaults → global → project `.plumb/config.toml` → project wins in **both directions** (the `generated_summaries` precedent), hot-reloaded, snapshotted per connection so the hot path never reads config per call, and surfaced with provenance in `plumb config show`. No new MCP tools; no env override (matching `[memory]`/`[session]`). Guarded by config tests (both override directions, negative-budget rejection, per-connection snapshot), peer-hint tests (happy path, disable-cleanly gating, recency-window cutoff, budget cap, no-path arg, recency-window resolution), and the topology-annotation / digest / clamp unit tests. First of three stacked phases (#150 → #151 → #152).

### Changed

- **Semantic re-rank for `topology_search` is now generally available.** The optional embedding-similarity re-rank (`[semantics]`, shipped behind a flag in 0.8.47) is promoted from an opt-in spike to a supported capability. Behaviour is unchanged — it stays **off by default** and **API / bring-your-own-endpoint only** (plumb never bundles, downloads, or supervises a model), because it requires an embedding endpoint you supply; FTS5 remains the authoritative ranking spine and any embedding error falls back to plain ranking (`mode=ranked`). What changes is the positioning and the documentation: the `[semantics]` configuration reference now presents the full provider matrix (`openai`/`voyage`/`jina`/`mistral`/`cohere`/`custom`), key precedence, the `topology.db` embedding cache, and the fallback contract as a stable surface rather than an experiment. See the [`[semantics]` configuration section](docs/configuration.md).

## 0.9.26 (2026-07-04)

### Changed

- **`plumb setup --all` now renders its results as a dotted table instead of space-padded lines.** The old output used `fmt.Sprintf("%-22s %s", …)` inside a context box, so a client managing more than one config path (Claude Desktop, whose sibling-profile fan-out joins each path's status with `; `) produced one very long status string that wrapped and misaligned in the terminal. `refreshClient` now returns structured per-path rows (`clientRow{name, status, detail}`) rather than a joined string, and `runSetupAll` feeds them through the shared `render.DottedTableBase` helper already used by `plumb sessions`/`plumb stats` — `Client | Status | Config` columns, one row per managed config path, with the client name blank on a multi-path client's continuation rows so its paths group visually. Status words are shortened to fit a column (`updated`/`already current`/`not registered`/`not installed`/`error`) and the config path (or error text) moves into its own aligned `Config` column. No behavioural change — the same clients are repointed. Guarded by the updated `TestRefreshClient` and `TestRefreshClient_MultiplePaths` (now asserting the structured rows).

### Added

- **Trusted per-workspace filesystem roots — grant a single workspace extra `extra_roots`/`read_roots` from the TUI, safely.** 0.9.24 closed a real escape by forcing a project `.plumb/config.toml`'s `[workspace] extra_roots`/`read_roots` back to the global base (a cloned hostile repo shipping `extra_roots = ["/"]` would otherwise gain read-write access outside the workspace the instant a session attached), which left roots global-only and the TUI Settings hiding those rows in a workspace scope. That was the right fix for the *untrusted, auto-applied* case, but it also blocked the legitimate one: a user deliberately granting one project access to an external folder. The danger was never a *manual* grant — it is a repo widening access with **zero user action**. Per-workspace roots now return, stored the safe way: a new **`config.WorkspaceRootsStore`** (`internal/config/workspace_roots.go`, mirroring `TrustStore`) records the grant in plumb's own data dir (`<DataDir>/workspace_roots.json`), keyed by the canonical workspace root — **never** in the repo. A cloned repository can neither write there nor change a granted path after the fact, so the grant is exactly the folders the user typed (the VS Code "workspace trust" model). `LoadProject`'s force-to-base is unchanged (defence in depth — even a *trusted* repo's config-file roots stay ignored; the out-of-repo store is the only way to widen access). The TUI Settings screen shows **Extra roots**/**Read roots** in a workspace scope again, editing the store (not the project TOML) and reusing the reload-project plumbing so the live daemon rebuilds its `PathPolicy` and re-reads the store; `buildPathPolicy` folds the grants into the per-connection allowlist (extra read-write as `workspace-root`, read read-only as `workspace-read-root`, additive to the config roots); and `plumb config show --workspace <dir>` surfaces the grants under the `workspace` section with a `data-dir grant` source for auditability. Guarded by `TestWorkspaceRootsStore_*` (round-trip, per-root isolation, empty-clears-and-prunes, read-error-fails-closed, **not-written-into-project**), `TestBuildPathPolicy_TrustedWorkspaceRoots` (granted roots admitted at the right access, an ungranted path still refused), and `TestWorkspaceRoots_EditsWriteStoreNotProject` (the TUI edit writes the store, not the project config, and reset clears it). `TestLoadProject_ForcesUntrustedSecurityFieldsToBase` stays green — the project-config escape remains closed.

## 0.9.25 (2026-07-04)

### Added

- **`run_task`'s parameter-alias table now accepts `task` as an alias for `slot`.** `paramAliases` (`internal/mcp/argalias.go`) had no entry for the common name an agent reaches for when asking to run a task, so `run_task({"task": "lint"})` was rejected client-side (against the published schema, before the daemon's own alias-tolerant resolution could run) rather than being interpreted as `{"slot": "lint"}`. Added `"task": {"slot"}` to the table, matching the existing empirically-driven pattern. Guarded by a new case in `TestResolveArgs_ExpandedAliases`.
- **Real-schema alias parity tests.** The alias-resolution tests exercised hand-written synthetic schemas only, so a quirk in a real tool's registered schema (one that `parseShape` could not guard, silently disabling aliases for that tool) or an alias entry that did not resolve against a tool's actual properties would pass the suite while failing in the field. `argalias_realschema_test.go` now drives full `tools/call` JSON-RPC round-trips (Serve → alias rewrite → real `Execute`) against the real `read_file`/`edit_file`/`write_file`/`delete_file`/`rename_file`/`list_files`/`search_in_files`/`run_task` tools with the field-reported alias spellings (`path`, `file`, `filename`, `filepath`, `dir`, `query`, `text`, `source`/`destination`, `old_str`/`new_str`, `task`), asserting the rewrite notice and the successful result.
- **The `AGENTS.md` tool count is now test-enforced.** The `## Available tools (N)` heading was a hand-maintained number with a history of drift (it read 55 while the registry held 51, then the registry caught up — nobody could tell which side was wrong without counting `srv.Register` calls). A new plain-unit `TestAgentsToolCount` (`internal/mcp/agents_toolcount_test.go`) asserts the documented count equals `len(selftestToolNames())` — the canonical coverage list that the integration parity guard (`TestSmoke_ToolListParity`) already pins to the live `tools/list`. Together the two checks close the loop: a tool added or removed without updating the heading now fails every `go test ./...`/`make verify`, not just the integration lane. The `add-mcp-tool` skill's checklist is updated to name the canonical list's location and both enforcing tests.

### Fixed

- **A `read_file`/`list_directory`/`list_files` call on a slow or unresponsive filesystem now fails fast instead of hanging to the client's multi-minute timeout.** These three tools discarded their `context` and performed blocking `os.Stat`/`os.Open`/`os.ReadDir`/`filepath.WalkDir` syscalls with no deadline, and the dispatcher (`handleToolsCall`) wrapped `Execute` in no timeout — so a stat/open on a stalled mount (a hung network, iCloud, or FUSE volume, or a contended disk) ran unbounded until the MCP client abandoned the call (~4 min for Claude Desktop). The existing `PLUMB_WRITE_TIMEOUT` could not help: it bounds the socket *write* of a finished response, and a wedged tool never produces one. (The LSP tools and `search_in_files`/`find_files` already self-bound; these were the outliers.) A tool may now opt into a dispatch-level execution deadline by implementing the marker interface `mcp.ExecTimeoutBounded`; `read_file`, `list_directory`, and `list_files` do. `execTool` runs such a tool on a child goroutine and returns an actionable error at the deadline (`… exceeded its 10s execution deadline — the target path may be on a slow or unresponsive filesystem …`) even if the orphaned syscall is still blocked; the derived `execCtx` also lets the three tools bail cooperatively (they now thread `ctx` and check it before/inside their stat/read/walk). The bound is applied only when the timeout is positive and the caller has not already set a deadline, so it never shortens a self-bounding LSP call or a cold-start handshake. Default **10 s**, overridable via `PLUMB_TOOL_EXEC_TIMEOUT` (a Go duration; `0`/`off` disables), wired on the `mcp.Server` exactly like `WriteTimeout`. Guarded by `TestExecTool_*` (slow tool times out at the bound and returns promptly; fast tool unaffected; `0` disables; an unopted tool is never bounded or given an injected deadline; a caller-supplied deadline is not shortened) and `TestServerToolExecTimeout` (env parsing).
- **The workspace pin is now sticky to the last EXPLICIT target, so reading a file in another project by absolute path can no longer silently re-pin a connection.** A user reported writing to project A, then — after a reconnect — having a write to A rejected with “pinned to /B”, with no explicit re-pin. Root cause: `persistPin` recorded the *last root touched*, including a path-seeded auto-attach (`onBeforeTool` pins an unpinned connection to whatever project the first tool path sits in), and on a client that reports no roots (Claude Desktop) a reconnect could come back unpinned and re-seed the pin from the next incidental read. Now only an **explicit** pin is persisted as the sticky target — a deliberate `session_start` `workspace` argument or a client-reported root; an auto-attach seeded from an incidental `file_path`/`path`/`uri` still sets the in-memory workspace for zero-config convenience but writes nothing durable, so it can never overwrite the explicit target. On reconnect the persisted explicit pin is rehydrated before any tool runs (existing `OnInit` path), and `onBeforeTool` now also restores it *before* seeding from an incidental path — so a reconnected connection that reads project B by absolute path lands back on the explicitly-chosen A rather than drifting to B. The boundary guard that caught the cross-project write is unchanged (it is correct). No schema change: the fix gates the existing persistence, it does not add columns. `attachWorkspace` splits into a thin explicit-by-default wrapper over `attachWorkspacePin(ctx, uri, explicit)`; `workspaceArgPresent` classifies the seed. Guarded by `TestWorkspaceArgPresent`, `TestPersist_AutoAttachDoesNotPersistPin`, `TestPersist_ExplicitAttachPersistsPin`, and `TestOnBeforeTool_IncidentalReadRestoresExplicitPin` (an incidental cross-project read on a reconnected connection restores the explicit pin).
- **`plumb serve` now logs WHY each daemon reconnect fires, not just that one did.** A user saw the `plumb daemon reconnected` note appear ~4 times in one session and had no way to tell whether each was a crash, a hang, or an idle-drop — the serve log recorded only *that* it reconnected. There are three reconnect triggers, and only the heartbeat-hang path was ever logged: a client→daemon write failure and a daemon→client read/EOF both called `reconnect` and discarded the underlying error. `reconnect` now takes a `reason` threaded from each call site — the write error, the daemon EOF (labelled *likely daemon crash or idle eviction; check daemon.log*, since the two are indistinguishable from the proxy side), or the heartbeat timeout — and logs it on both the per-attempt failure entries and the `serve: reconnected to daemon after failure` success entry. So four reconnect notes now come with four attributable causes. (The daemon side already logs `daemon: evicting idle session`, so an idle-drop is confirmable by cross-referencing `daemon.log`; the serve-side EOF reason points there rather than guessing.) Guarded by `TestProxyReconnect_LogsReason`.
- **`read_file`/`list_directory`/`list_files` now accept a `uri` argument, closing the last gap in the path-parameter alias set.** The three names for a file/dir location — `file_path` (content tools), `uri` (LSP tools), `path` (search/dir tools) — were only partially cross-accepted: passing `uri` to `read_file` (a natural carry-over after a `file_outline` call) errored, because `paramAliases` had no `uri` key. (The reverse, `file_path` on a `uri`-canonical tool, already worked — the table is keyed post-normalisation, and `file_path` normalises to the existing `filepath` entry.) Added `"uri": {"file_path", "path", "root"}`, so `uri` now resolves to whichever of those a tool actually declares, with the usual one-line alias notice. The eligibility rule is unchanged, so a tool whose real parameter *is* `uri` (the LSP tools) is untouched — `rewriteObject` skips a key that is already a declared parameter. Guarded by the new `uri → file_path` / `uri → path` / `uri → root` cases in `TestResolveArgs`.
- **`plumb setup claude-desktop` and `plumb setup --all` now also repoint a sibling Claude Desktop profile, so `--all` can no longer report `already current` while a live profile is actually stale.** Anthropic documents exactly one `claude_desktop_config.json` path per OS; a user running two Claude accounts side by side via the unofficial `--user-data-dir` flag or a duplicated `.app` bundle ends up with a second profile directory (e.g. `Claude-Personal`) plumb never looked at, so `setup --all` correctly reported the canonical path as current while the account the user actually launches stayed unregistered. `claudeDesktopConfigPaths` now returns the canonical path plus a heuristic scan for any existing sibling `Claude*/claude_desktop_config.json` (a naming-convention match, not an Anthropic-documented mechanism, and explicitly commented as such); `setupTarget` gained an optional `pathsFn` so `refreshClient`/`setup --all` fan out across every discovered profile instead of just one, and `plumb setup claude-desktop` reports per-path status. `plumb doctor` gained the matching `checkClaudeDesktopExtraProfiles` (mirroring the existing Antigravity legacy-config check) so a stale binary in a sibling profile is flagged instead of passing silently. Guarded by `TestClaudeDesktopExtraConfigPaths_DiscoversOnlyExistingSiblingProfiles`, `TestClaudeDesktopExtraConfigPaths_NoneFound`, `TestClaudeDesktopConfigPaths_CanonicalFirstThenExtras`, `TestRefreshClient_MultiplePaths`, and `TestCheckClaudeDesktopExtraProfiles`.
### Docs

- **Contributor procedures extracted from `AGENTS.md` into project skills.** "How to add an LSP adapter", "How to add an MCP tool", and "Tool implementation pattern" (the `Execute()` skeleton) were always-loaded prose that only mattered when a contributor was actually adding an adapter or a tool. They now live as two on-demand project skills readable as plain markdown from any client — `.claude/skills/add-lsp-adapter/SKILL.md` and `.claude/skills/add-mcp-tool/SKILL.md` — and `AGENTS.md` replaces the three sections with a short "## Contributor recipes" pointer, shrinking by ~30 lines. Phase 2 of the skills strategy (`private/docs/internal/skills-strategy.md` in plumb-ops); the shipped user-facing skill set under `internal/cli/skills/` is untouched.

## 0.9.24 (2026-07-02)

### Added

- **plumb now pins its core tools into Claude Code's context so the client's MCP tool search never defers them behind a `ToolSearch` round-trip.** Claude Code defers MCP tool *schemas* by default — at session start only tool *names* load, and the model must call `ToolSearch` to page a tool's schema in before invoking it. Until it does, a direct call with guessed parameters is rejected *client-side, before the request ever reaches plumb* ("'plumb:read_file' has not been loaded yet … Call tool_search first"), so plumb's own parameter-alias/arg-tolerance layer cannot help — the block is one layer above it. plumb now advertises its highest-frequency tools with `_meta["anthropic/alwaysLoad"] = true` in the `tools/list` response (`MetaAlwaysLoadKey = "anthropic/alwaysLoad"`), which Claude Code (v2.1.121+) reads to load those tools into context up front instead of deferring them. A new `mcp.Server.AlwaysLoad func(name string) bool` field — set before `Serve`, consulted per `tools/list` with the registry lock released, exactly like the existing `ToolFilter` — decides which advertised tools are pinned; `handleToolsList` emits the `_meta` only for accepted names (via `_meta,omitempty`, so a non-pinned entry stays byte-identical to the pre-change payload). It is wired to `tools.IsLean` in `conn_register.go`, so the pinned set is **exactly `LeanTools`** — one list now serving double duty (lean-profile visibility *and* the never-deferred set), keeping the ~21 core tools always available while the ~34 long-tail tools stay deferred to preserve the context saving. The key deliberately uses Anthropic's `anthropic/` namespace (not plumb's `dev.plumbkit/…`) because it is a client-recognised key; clients that predate the convention ignore the unknown `_meta` and are unaffected. No config surface is added (a blunt per-machine override remains `alwaysLoad: true` on the plumb server entry in the client's own MCP config). Guarded by `TestToolsList_AlwaysLoadMeta` (pinned tool carries the `_meta`, unpinned does not) and the extended `TestServer_ToolsList` (no `_meta` when `AlwaysLoad` is unset).
- **Post-write diagnostics now catch cross-file breakage — when an edit introduces errors in files OTHER than the one written, plumb says so.** The post-write `diagnostics after write:` block only ever inspected the edited file's own URI, so the classic "change a signature, silently break its callers in other files" case produced a clean-looking write response and the agent moved on. Write tools now capture a whole-workspace error baseline *before* the bytes change (`newDiagBaseline`, via the routing invalidator's already-workspace-scoped `AllDiagnostics`/`AllDiagnosticTimes`), and after the edited file's own diagnostics land they run a bounded cross-file sweep that appends a `⚠ this edit introduced new errors in N other file(s)` heads-up naming each newly-broken file, its error-count delta, and a representative new error. Two guards keep it false-alarm-resistant: a **baseline diff** (a file is reported only if its error count ROSE versus the pre-write snapshot, so pre-existing errors are never re-flagged as fresh breakage) and a **publish-time check** (only files the language server re-published *after* the write are attributed, so an untouched file is never blamed); the sweep is additionally skipped when the edited file itself did not re-publish fresh (the server is lagging, so any delta is unreliable). The single-file block keeps priority — it is built and returned first and is never delayed or dropped — and the sweep waits only a bounded settle grace (`[edits].post_write_cross_file_settle_ms`, default 200 ms; `0` compares immediately) for dependent-file re-publishes before comparing, all managed daemon-internally within the one tool response. The wording never over-claims: it states the delta, hedges the mid-series-refactor case, and points at `diagnostics()` to confirm — deliberately not resurrecting the alarmist "I just broke the build" phrasing removed earlier. Controlled by `[edits].post_write_cross_file` (default on; env `PLUMB_POST_WRITE_CROSS_FILE` / `PLUMB_POST_WRITE_CROSS_FILE_SETTLE_MS`), surfaced in `plumb config show` and the TUI Settings (Editing group). Guarded by `TestComputeCrossFileDelta` (new-file/count-rise/unchanged/pre-existing/lagging-timestamp/edited-URI-excluded/warning-ignored cases), `TestFormatCrossFileDiagnostics` (relativised paths, delta wording, overflow), `TestWriteDeps_crossFileDiagnostics` (end-to-end incl. fresh=false / nil-baseline / disabled suppression), and the `internal/config` default/validate/env tests.
- **A daemon restart is now transparent to a connected agent — strict-mode read-tracking and the pinned workspace survive it.** `plumb serve` already kept the client connected across a `plumb daemon` restart and replayed the `initialize` handshake, but all daemon-side per-connection state was in-memory and lost: in strict mode the first `edit_file` after a restart was refused with "has not been read in this daemon session" until the file was re-read, and a client that reports no roots (e.g. Claude Desktop) came back unpinned. `plumb serve` now generates a stable per-process **proxy session ID** (`crypto/rand` UUIDv4), injects it into the captured `initialize` frame's `params._meta["dev.plumbkit/proxy-session-id"]` (alongside the existing allow-dirs, via a single combined injector), and replays it on every reconnect. The daemon persists read-tracking (path → mtime + content SHA, scoped by `(proxy session, workspace)`) and the pinned workspace to a new `session_state.db` (in the data dir, beside `stats.db`; a dedicated store, **not** the drop-on-overflow stats writer), keyed by that ID. On reconnect the fresh daemon recognises the continuation and rehydrates: a strict-mode edit of an unchanged file read before the restart now passes, and an unpinned reconnect re-pins itself. **Safe by construction** — a rehydrated read still flows through `checkStrictRead`'s on-disk `os.Stat`+mtime comparison, so it can only satisfy a byte-identical file, never bypass a dirty-file check; workspace-scoping means a re-pin to a different project never resurrects the old project's reads; in-flight **writes** are still never auto-replayed. Controlled by `[session].persist_state` (default on; env `PLUMB_PERSIST_SESSION_STATE`) and `persist_state_ttl_minutes` (config-only, default 24h; `0` disables pruning), the latter reclaiming state left by a serve proxy that died without reconnecting, independent of `eviction_ttl_minutes`. Guarded by the `internal/sessionstate` store tests (round-trip incl. nanosecond mtime fidelity, per-session isolation, workspace-scoping, TTL prune), `ReadTracker` sink/`Hydrate` tests, `mcp.TestProxySessionFromParams`, the serve-side `TestInjectInitMeta_*`/`TestNewProxySessionIDFormat` tests, and the `internal/cli` `TestPersist_*` restart-survival/isolation/repin/pin-rehydration/disabled tests.

### Fixed

- **The dashboard's lifetime "Token Efficiency" block now shows the capability-vs-efficiency split instead of a permanently-full bar.** Both block-grids in the Dashboard Token Efficiency panel rendered `tokenSavingsBar`'s progress-toward-1.5M-tokens fill: the left grid against current-daemon savings (meaningful, it varies), but the right grid against the all-time lifetime total — which is virtually always far above the 1.5 M target, so it saturated to 100% bright after the first busy session and conveyed nothing (it looked identical for every heavy user). The right grid now renders the honest capability/efficiency composition it already captions (`tokenSavingsSplitRow`): every column is lit, apportioned by each axis's share of the lifetime total (a non-zero axis always shows at least one column; zero total renders dim), capability in the success colour and efficiency in the accent colour, with the `cap`/`eff` caption words colour-matched as a legend. The left grid, the compact header meter, and `tokenSavingsBar` itself are unchanged. Guarded by `TestSplitGroups` (apportioning, slivers, clamping, sum-to-groups) and `TestTokenSavingsSplitRow` (column count, per-axis colour counts, dim empty row).
- **Topology DB `busy_timeout` and `foreign_keys` now apply to every pooled connection, so `ON DELETE CASCADE` actually fires.** `openDB` opened the SQLite database on a bare path and set `PRAGMA busy_timeout`/`foreign_keys` via `db.Exec` — but those are PER-CONNECTION pragmas, and `database/sql` pools connections (the background indexer's writes run concurrently with read-tool queries on the shared handle). Only the one connection that happened to serve the `Exec` had foreign keys enabled; every other pooled connection ran with `foreign_keys = OFF`. Edge cleanup relies entirely on cascade (`deleteFileNodes`/prune delete only `topology_nodes`, never `topology_edges`), so a delete that landed on an FK-off connection silently left the file's edges behind — orphan `topology_edges` accumulated on every re-index/prune, and `busy_timeout = 0` on those connections turned recoverable writer contention into an immediate `database is locked`. The three pragmas now travel in the DSN (`_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)&_pragma=foreign_keys(1)&_pragma=journal_mode(WAL)`), which the driver applies on every new connection — matching how `internal/stats` already opens its database. Guarded by `TestOpenDB_PragmasApplyToEveryPooledConnection` (forces four concurrent pooled connections and asserts `foreign_keys=1`/`busy_timeout=5000` on each).
- **Semantic edits (`replace_symbol_body`/`insert_before`/`insert_after`/`safe_delete_symbol`/`rename_symbol`) now take the per-path write lock and write through a unique temp file, closing a lost-update / torn-write race.** `applyTextEditsToFile` read the file, applied the edits, and wrote `<path>.tmp` then renamed — with no `lockPath`, unlike `write_file`/`edit_file`. Because the daemon dispatches tool calls concurrently across connections, a `replace_symbol_body` racing an `edit_file` (or two symbol edits) on the same file could each read the same pre-edit content and silently overwrite the other's result, breaking the documented "per-path locks across all write tools" guarantee. Worse, the temp name was a fixed `<path>.tmp`, so two concurrent writers to one file wrote and renamed the *same* temp — corrupting or truncating it. The apply path now acquires the per-path lock and writes through `safeWrite` (uniquely-named temp + atomic rename, symlink-aware), with the lock taken/released per file so a multi-file `rename_symbol` never holds two locks at once (no lock-ordering deadlock). Guarded by `TestApplyTextEditsToFile_ConcurrentNoLostUpdate` (8 concurrent prepends must all survive; runs under `-race`).
- **`find_replace` no longer reads or writes through an in-tree symlink that points outside the workspace, and now warns when the `max_files` cap truncates the result.** (1) Every other write tool boundary-checks each resolved target path, but `find_replace` checked only the root argument — a directory walk that encountered a symlink to an external file would `safeWrite` *through* it (the resolver follows the link), silently mutating a file outside the pinned workspace and defeating the by-construction PathPolicy write boundary. The per-file worker now `Lstat`s each candidate and, for a symlink, runs the symlink-resolving boundary check (only a symlink can escape a walked in-boundary root, so regular files pay nothing), skipping any whose target lies outside the workspace — closing both the write escape and the dry-run preview's read of an external target. (2) When more matching files existed than `max_files`, the response reported `N file(s) changed` with no hint that the cap had silently dropped the rest; it now appends a `⚠ reached max_files=N — additional matching file(s) were NOT modified` warning, and the candidate list is sorted so the budget *prefers* the lowest-path files (this only biases the selection — the parallel workers race on the budget counter, so the truncated set is not guaranteed identical between a preview and the apply). Guarded by `TestFindReplace_SkipsSymlinkEscapingWorkspace` and `TestFindReplace_WarnsOnMaxFilesTruncation`.
- **The web UI's `GET /api/settings` no longer leaks the configured `semantics.api_key` in its response.** The settings model serialised every registry field's resolved value verbatim, and `semantics.api_key` is a registered string field — so the literal embedding-provider key was echoed into the JSON response body (landing in browser memory/devtools), even though the endpoint is loopback+token gated and the MCP `agent_config` path deliberately excludes it. The config field registry gains a `Secret` flag; `semantics.api_key` is marked secret, and the web settings surface now redacts secret fields to a fixed mask sentinel (`••••••••` when set, empty when unset) instead of the literal value. Because the settings are editable (`POST /api/settings`), the write path also treats an incoming value equal to the mask as an unchanged no-op, so a blind form re-submit can never round-trip the mask into the stored config. The TUI's local settings display is unaffected (it does not serialise to a client). Guarded by `TestSettings_RedactsSemanticsAPIKey` and `TestSettingsSet_RedactedSentinelIsNoOp`.
- **An untrusted project `.plumb/config.toml` can no longer widen the filesystem-access allowlist or redirect the semantics embedding endpoint/credentials.** A cloned hostile repo shipping `[workspace] extra_roots = ["/"]` previously gained read-WRITE access outside the pinned workspace the instant a session attached — no confirmation — defeating the "a write outside the workspace is refused by construction" invariant; and `[semantics] provider/base_url/api_key_env` turned a routine `topology_search` into an SSRF + environment-secret-exfiltration primitive (the resolver runs `os.Getenv` on the attacker-named variable and the client POSTs it as a bearer token to the attacker-named URL). `LoadProject` already forced `agent_config_writes`/`[web]`/`[ui]` back to the trusted global base for exactly this "a cloned repo ships it" threat model; it now also forces `[semantics]` and `[workspace] extra_roots`/`read_roots` back to base, closing the filesystem-boundary escape and the semantics SSRF/exfil vector while leaving benign per-project overrides (e.g. `edits.rate_limit_per_minute`) intact. These roots are global-only — set them in global config — consistent with the `agent_config` tool already treating them as un-writable, and the TUI Settings now shows `extra_roots`/`read_roots` only in the Global scope (a workspace-scope override would never take effect). Guarded by `TestLoadProject_ForcesUntrustedSecurityFieldsToBase`.
- **`git`-tool network-tier hardening: protected-branch force-push enforcement and ad-hoc-URL refusal across `push`/`fetch`/`pull`.** (1) `checkPushProtection` only treated `-f`/`--force` as a force push, so `git push origin +main` (git's `+`-prefixed refspec force form) bypassed the protected-branch guard; a `+`-prefixed positional refspec now also counts as a force. (2) The protected-branch match is lexical, so a force push that targets the current branch *without naming an explicit safe destination* — `git push origin +HEAD`, a bare `git push -f origin` (push.default), or `git push -f -o ci.skip origin` (a value-taking push option that shifts naïve positional parsing, so the remote was misread and the force allowed) — must be caught without resolving git's symbolic HEAD. The guard now refuses a force push, when any branch is protected, **unless it names an explicit destination refspec whose target branch is neither protected nor `HEAD`** (safe-bias, robust to arg parsing: the remote is identified with push flag-value arity awareness — `-o`/`--push-option`/`--repo`/`--receive-pack`/`--exec` consume the following arg — and a force with no provably-safe destination is *rejected*, not allowed). (3) The ad-hoc-URL/remote-helper refusal — which blocks the `git fetch ext::sh -c <cmd>` RCE vector — was applied only to `push` and matched only `ext::`; it now covers **every** network subcommand and any generic `<transport>::` helper form. All opt-in (require `allow_push` + `confirm`). Guarded by `TestCheckPushProtection` (force `+main`/`+feature:main`/`+HEAD`/bare-`-f`/`-o ci.skip origin`/`+main:feature`, generic `::` helper, plus the allowed `+feature`/`+HEAD:feature`) and `TestCheckPushProtection_NetworkSubcommandURLRefusal`.
- **The stats and session-state SQLite databases now actually apply `busy_timeout` and WAL.** `internal/stats` and `internal/sessionstate` opened their databases with the mattn-style `?_busy_timeout=5000&_journal_mode=WAL` DSN params — which the **modernc** driver this project uses *silently ignores* (verified: that DSN yields `busy_timeout=0`, `journal_mode=delete`). So both ran with no busy timeout and in rollback-journal mode rather than WAL, defeating WAL's concurrent-reader benefit (the stats read-only handle vs the writer) and turning any lock contention into an immediate `database is locked` instead of a 5s wait. Both now use the `_pragma=busy_timeout(...)&_pragma=journal_mode(WAL)` form the driver honours — the same fix #122 applied to topology (whose note mistakenly cited stats as already correct). Guarded by `stats.TestOpen_AppliesBusyTimeoutAndWAL` and `sessionstate.TestOpenAt_AppliesBusyTimeoutAndWAL`.
- **`config.Save` no longer bakes an active `PLUMB_*` environment override into `config.toml`.** `Save` loaded the config via `Load`, which applies the env overlay, then re-encoded the whole struct — so changing one global setting in the TUI (e.g. the log level) while, say, `PLUMB_WRITE_RATE_LIMIT` was set silently persisted that transient env value into the file as if the user had chosen it, where it then outlived the env var. `Save` now loads via `loadForSave` (compiled defaults + the on-disk file only, **no** env overlay), so a full-struct save can never write an environment override back into the file. (Single-key writes already had the sparse, env-free `SetGlobalValue`/`SaveTheme` path; this closes the whole-struct path that the other global Settings rows use.) Guarded by `TestSave_DoesNotBakeEnvOverride`.
- **The semantics embedding clients now bound the response body they read, so a misbehaving or hostile endpoint cannot OOM the daemon.** `openAICompatible.Embed` and `cohere.Embed` did `io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` with no size cap; the `http.Client` bounds time, not bytes, so an endpoint could stream an arbitrarily large body within the timeout and force the shared daemon to allocate it all into one slice (remotely triggerable when, before the companion fix, a project `[semantics] base_url` could point the client at an attacker URL). Both now read through a shared `readCapped` (`io.LimitReader`, 16 MiB cap) and treat an over-limit body as an error, so `topology_search` falls back to its FTS5 baseline rather than buffering an unbounded response. Guarded by `TestReadCapped`.
- **LSP supervisor: the OnStart-failure restart path no longer leaks two pipe FDs per attempt.** On an `OnStart` handshake failure the supervisor killed the process and called `proc.Process.Wait()` (`os.Process.Wait`), which does not close the `exec.Cmd`'s stdin/stdout parent pipe ends or join its IO goroutines — so a server that repeatedly fails its cold-start (a misconfigured rust-analyzer/jdtls) leaked two FDs per backoff attempt until GC. It now calls `proc.Wait()` (`exec.Cmd.Wait`), matching the normal-exit path. (`lsp-3`)
- **`git` tool: removed the unreachable `-c`/`-C` tokens from the `branch` classifier.** `classifyBranch` listed `-c`/`-C` (branch copy) as write-tier, but those short flags are rejected by the global-flag denylist (they collide with git's `-c`/`-C` config-injection flags) before classification ever runs, so the tokens were dead code implying a path that does not work. Branch copy is reached via the long `--copy` form, which is unaffected. (`toolsmisc-3`)
- **Episodic session summaries no longer count a FAILED mutation as a modification.** `buildEpisodicDetail` tallied every `edit_file`/`write_file`/`transaction_apply`/applied-`find_replace` call into `WriteN`/Touched/SourcePaths regardless of whether it succeeded, so a session whose write was rejected (rate-limited, dirty-file, boundary violation) was summarised as having modified files it never changed. Failed mutations are now excluded from the write tally and the touched/source-path lists (reads are still counted). Guarded by `TestBuildEpisodicDetail_ExcludesFailedWrite`. (`cli-1`)
- **`plumb stop` no longer risks signalling an unrelated process.** The pgrep fallback matched any process whose argv merely contained the substring `plumb daemon` (e.g. `vim plumb daemon.go`). Each candidate is now verified via `ps` to be a real `plumb daemon` (executable basename `plumb`, first arg `daemon`) before it is signalled. (`cli-3`)
- **The `[quality]` post-write analysis (golangci-lint findings appended to write responses) actually runs now — it was dead on arrival.** `buildWriteDeps` captured the quality runner eagerly: `if r := s.view().qualityRunner; r != nil { qualityReport = r.Report }`. But `buildWriteDeps` runs during tool registration (`handleConn` → `registerAllTools`), **before** the client handshake attaches the workspace and creates the runner (`startQualityRunner` at attach) — so the runner was always nil at capture, `WriteDeps.QualityReport` stayed permanently nil, and the whole feature silently never fired despite a green build (its unit tests exercise the `Runner` directly, never the wiring). The identical eager-capture-nil hazard was already fixed one line below for topology (`topologyNotify` resolves the store per-write) but missed for quality. `qualityReport` is now the same lazy closure, resolving `s.view().qualityRunner` on each write. Guarded by `TestBuildWriteDeps_QualityReportIsLazy`.
- **The web UI rejects a project-settings write to a non-workspace path, and no longer rejects every write when opened via `http://localhost`.** Two `internal/web` fixes: **(web-2)** `POST /api/settings` at a project scope passed `req.Scope` straight to `SetProjectValue`, so an arbitrary scope would drop a `.plumb/config.toml` at any path on disk; the scope is now validated against the currently-attached workspaces (`isActiveWorkspace`) and an unknown scope is a 400. **(web-3)** the CSRF same-origin guard compared the request Origin/Host against the bound `127.0.0.1:<port>` by exact string, so opening the UI via `http://localhost:<port>` (or `[::1]`) made every state-changing request fail as cross-origin; it now accepts any loopback host (127.0.0.1 / localhost / ::1) on the bound port while still rejecting a genuine foreign origin or a wrong port. Guarded by `TestSettingsSet_RejectsUnknownWorkspaceScope` and `TestSameOrigin_AcceptsLoopbackEquivalents`.
- **`GET /api/settings` masks credentials embedded in a URL-valued setting (e.g. `semantics.base_url`).** A `base_url` such as `http://user:pass@host` is user-typed config, not a dedicated secret, so it is intentionally not marked `Secret` (the user wants to see the endpoint) — but its embedded userinfo would otherwise be echoed verbatim into the settings response. The web settings surface now redacts the userinfo of any URL-valued field (rendering `http://redacted@host/v1`) while keeping the rest of the URL visible; non-URL and credential-free values are untouched. Guarded by `TestRedactURLUserinfo`.
- **A second connection attaching to a workspace can no longer roll back a live `transaction_apply` running on it from another connection.** `txlog.Scan` (orphan-transaction recovery) ran on every workspace attach/re-pin and unconditionally rolled back *every* `.plumb/tx-log/*` directory it found — with no way to tell a crashed-daemon orphan from a transaction that is in flight right now. Because the daemon is shared across connections, if connection A was mid-transaction (its tx-log dir on disk, files being written under per-path locks) when connection B attached the same workspace, B's `Scan` reverted A's already-written files to their pre-write snapshots and deleted A's log — silent partial corruption, with A still returning success. `Scan` now takes the daemon's start time as a cutoff and skips any tx-log directory whose manifest `StartedAt` is at or after it. To make that cutoff reliable, `writeManifest` is now **atomic** (unique temp + `rename`, fsync'd) — a `Record` during a live multi-file transaction rewrites the manifest on every step, and a concurrent `Scan` `os.ReadFile`-ing a half-written manifest would `Unmarshal`-fail, miss the `StartedAt≥cutoff` guard, and treat the live txn as a recoverable orphan; the atomic write guarantees a reader always sees a complete manifest (old or new), so the cutoff is never bypassed for a live transaction. A directory with an unreadable/absent `StartedAt` (a crash before the first manifest write, or a corrupt previous-run orphan) is still treated as a recoverable orphan. Guarded by `TestScan_SkipsCurrentRunButRollsBackOrphan` and `TestWriteManifest_AtomicUnderConcurrentScan` (a `-race` test running `Scan` concurrently with in-flight `Record`s).
- **A stalled language-server write no longer wedges every later LSP call, server notifications are delivered in wire order, and a cancelled call always reaches the server as `$/cancelRequest`.** Three JSON-RPC transport (`internal/lsp/jsonrpc`) concurrency fixes: **(lsp-1)** `Call` wrote the request synchronously while holding the write lock, so if the server stopped draining its stdin pipe (saturated/wedged, OS buffer full) the write blocked forever holding the lock — and because acquiring the lock *precedes* the ctx-aware response wait, the `[lsp_query]` deadline could not rescue it: every subsequent call on that connection hung. All writes now go through `sendCtx`, which performs the raw write in a goroutine and returns early on ctx-cancel or connection-close, and runs a stall watchdog: a write that blocks past `writeStallTimeout` (lowered to 15 s, kept distinctly below the default 30 s `[lsp_query]` deadline so a wedged write is torn down *before* the request times out rather than racing it) means a wedged server, so the connection is closed — unblocking every pending call with a clear error and letting the pool tear it down — instead of leaking the held lock. **(lsp-2)** server notifications were each dispatched in a fresh goroutine, so back-to-back `publishDiagnostics` for the same URI (the empty-then-real set gopls/rust-analyzer emit during indexing) could be reordered and leave the stale empty set winning, and a notification flood spawned unbounded goroutines; they now flow through a single in-order delivery goroutine fed by a bounded queue. **(lsp-4)** the cancel path had a CI-only deadlock: `Call` sent the request through `sendCtx(ctx, …)`, and when the write completed and `ctx` was cancelled in the same instant the watchdog `select` could pick `ctx.Done()` over the just-finished write and return `ctx.Err()` *before* the response-wait `select` ran — so `Call` returned without ever emitting `$/cancelRequest`, and a peer awaiting that frame blocked forever (only under scheduling load, so it deadlocked the cancel test under full-suite `-race` yet passed in isolation; reproduced locally with `GOMAXPROCS=1` and `-race -count`). `Call` now writes the request with `context.Background()` so cancellation flows solely through the response-wait `select`, which always runs after a successful send and emits `$/cancelRequest`; a ctx-already-cancelled pre-check avoids putting a doomed request on the wire. Guarded by `TestConn_WriteStallClosesConn`, `TestConn_NotificationsDeliveredInOrder`, and `TestConn_ContextCancel_AlwaysSendsCancelRequest_UnderLoad` (which pins `GOMAXPROCS=1` and fails on iteration 0 against the pre-fix code); all run under `-race`, and the existing `TestConn_Notify_ContextCancelUnblocks` still passes.
- **Topology read-only status handle now applies `busy_timeout` — the third instance of the modernc DSN bug (after #122/#133).** `StatusForWorkspace` (backing `topology_status` and the CLI status read while the daemon holds the writer) opened the index read-only with the mattn-style `?mode=ro&_busy_timeout=2000` DSN, which the modernc SQLite driver silently ignores, so the handle ran with `busy_timeout=0` — turning recoverable writer contention into an immediate `database is locked`. Switched to the `_pragma=busy_timeout(2000)` form. Guarded by `TestStatusForWorkspace_BusyTimeoutApplied`.
- **Web read endpoints now validate the `?workspace=` param against the active workspaces (read-side counterpart to the settings-write guard).** `/api/topology`, `/api/memory`, and `/api/memory/{name}` passed the raw `workspace` query value straight to `topology.StatusForWorkspace`/`memory.List`/`memory.Read` via `resolveWorkspace`, so a loopback+token-authenticated caller could read any on-disk path's `.plumb/` index or memories by naming it. `resolveWorkspace` now rejects an explicit workspace that is not a currently-attached session (the same `isActiveWorkspace` check the settings-write path uses), and the handlers return 400. Guarded by `TestReadEndpoints_RejectUnknownWorkspace`.

### Docs

- **Website and `AGENTS.md` trued up to the shipped code.** `site/index.html`: the adapter table and the LSP/"two engines" captions now show TypeScript/JS and Zig as **validated** (not experimental — both pass the real-binary integration tests since the `publishDiagnostics` capability fix); the Clients section advertises **thirteen** setup targets and adds the **Antigravity Desktop** chip; the seven tool-group badges now sum to the headline **55** (Read ×7→×8 for `file_status`, Edit ×12→×13 for `undo_edit`); and the footer version placeholder is bumped to v0.9.23. `AGENTS.md` (and its `CLAUDE.md`/`GEMINI.md` symlinks): the "Memory bounds" default soft heap limit is corrected from 4 GiB to the **1 GiB** the code actually applies (`defaultDaemonMemLimit`). Found by the autonomous review (`website-1/2/3/4/5`, `cli-2`).

## 0.9.23 (2026-06-29)

First tagged release. Automated cross-platform binaries — macOS (Intel + Apple Silicon) and Linux (Intel + ARM) — plus a Homebrew tap now ship from the release pipeline on every `v*` tag.

### Added

- **`edit_file` gains an anchor-bounded edit mode: replace the span between two unique anchors instead of an exact `old_string`.** As an alternative to the `edits` array, a call may pass `start_anchor` + `end_anchor` (two unique substrings/lines) and a `new_string` that replaces the span they bound; `include_anchors=false` (default) rewrites only the text *between* the anchors and keeps them as stable boundaries, `include_anchors=true` replaces the whole inclusive span. The two request shapes are mutually exclusive — `validateMode` rejects supplying both, or neither. Each anchor must match **exactly once** and `end_anchor` must occur after (and not overlap) `start_anchor`, with the same uniqueness/not-found errors as the `old_string` matcher; matching mirrors `str_replace` exactly — CRLF-tolerant and forgiving of a pasted display-only read_file gutter (`<n>\t`, multi-line consecutive prefixes), surfacing the same advisory note when a gutter is stripped. The mode lowers the anchors into a single synthetic `str_replace` edit (the full inclusive span, which carries both unique anchors and is therefore itself unique) and flows through the **same** write path as `edits` — per-path lock, `expected_mtime`/`expected_sha` guards, retry loop, LSP notify, cache invalidation, diff output, and write-rate budget — so only the span computation is new. Ideal for rewriting a block whose interior changes but whose boundary lines are stable. Guarded by `TestEditFileAnchor_*` (between/inclusive/empty-delete happy paths, not-found/ambiguous/end-before-start/overlap/both-modes/neither failures, gutter-aware, CRLF, and an existing-mode regression) and `TestBuildAnchorEdit_SpanIsUnique`.
- **The TUI Settings screen now exposes the `[memory]` Advanced Memory Engine knobs as editable rows.** The eight scalar/bool fields of `[memory]` (`enabled`, `generated_summaries`, `inject_hints`, `hint_budget_bytes`, `episodic_budget_bytes`, `max_hints`, `idle_summary_minutes`, `generated_memory_keep`) were settable only by hand-editing config TOML — every other config section already had Settings rows. They now appear under a new **Memory** group (toggles for the three bools, number rows for the five ints), wired through the same scope-aware persistence (global config or a workspace's `.plumb/config.toml`), reload-tier marker (next-session), and registry-stamped help as the existing rows. Backed by new entries in the config field registry (`internal/config/fields_registry.go`), so `plumb config show` and the agent-config validator see them too; `TestSettingsRegistryDrift` keeps the registry and the rows in lock-step. `intField`/`toggleLabel` were split (mirroring the existing `boolField`/`boolFieldMore`) to stay under the gocyclo-15 contract.
